note: Authored for the client prototype. These two modules are NOT units of the Kenyan Carpentry & Joinery Level 4 qualification — every one of its eight units assumes the learner already has tools and joints. They are the foundation that feeds it, so each criterion below carries `leadsTo`: the Level 4 unit codes it prepares the learner for. Nothing here claims Level 4 delivery.
source: Sokoine University of Agriculture, Faculty of Agriculture, Department of Agricultural Engineering and Land Planning — Workshop Technology Manual: Carpentry and Joinery, F. C. Kahimba, March 2010. Lessons 1 and 2. Structure and terminology.

terminology: UK / East African. Tenon saw, try square, marking gauge, smoothing plane, mm.

assessmentModes.knowledge: The platform can assess this in full.
assessmentModes.both: The platform assesses the knowledge half; an assessor signs off the performance at the bench.
assessmentModes.practical: The platform teaches and rehearses it; competence is assessed ONLY at the bench. The app must never report this as certified.

weightingNote: The Level 4 curriculum this feeds sets theory:practical at 30:70 and requires a portfolio of evidence and third-party reports. The assessmentMode split below is written to respect that: the majority of criteria here are `both` or `practical`, and the app is honest about owning the theory.

leadsToFramework.title: Carpentry and Joinery Level 4 (Kenya, TVET CDACC)

modules.title: Carpentry Foundation
modules.description: The hand tools of the trade, how they are kept, how the workshop is kept safe, and how a piece of timber is brought to size.

criteria.text: Group hand tools by what they do: measuring and marking, cutting, planing, boring, striking, holding.
Name the parts of a tenon saw, a smoothing plane, a firmer chisel, a try square and a marking gauge.
Select the right saw for a cut: rip saw along the grain, tenon saw for small accurate cuts and tenons, dovetail saw for fine work, frame saw for straight and curved cuts.
criteria.evidence: Tool selection observed at the bench.

criteria.text: Choose a mallet rather than a claw hammer when striking a chisel or a wooden surface, and say why.

units.title: Care for and maintain hand tools

criteria.text: Inspect a tool for defects before use and decide whether it is repaired, replaced or fit to use.
Identify a mushroomed striking head, a split handle, a loose head and a blunt edge as faults, and state the risk each carries.
Grind and sharpen a cutting edge to give a clean cut, and protect the edge in storage.
Store tools clean, dry and free of rust, and carry them safely between bench and site.

units.title: Work safely in the carpentry workshop

criteria.text: Select and wear the personal protective equipment a task requires: eye protection, hearing protection, dust mask, gloves, safety boots.
State and follow the rules for hand tools: cut away from the body, never hold work in the palm, never use a tool for a job it was not made for.
State and follow the rules for power machines: guards in position, keys removed, stock checked for nails, push stick used, power isolated before any adjustment.
criteria.evidence: Written test; assessor sign-off before machine access.

criteria.text: Identify why loose clothing, jewellery and gloves are hazards near rotating blades.
Keep the work area clear, swept and well lit, and explain how housekeeping prevents slips, trips and falls.
Select timber for a job, softwood or hardwood, large enough that unnecessary joints are avoided.
Mark raw timber to the required dimensions, leaving allowance for sawing and planing.
Plane a face side straight, then a face edge straight and square to it, and mark both.
criteria.evidence: Assessor sign-off; checked with try square and straight edge.

criteria.text: Set a marking gauge from the face side and face edge to gauge width and thickness.
Plane to the gauge lines to reach final dimensions, sawing first where the waste is heavy.

modules.title: Carpentry Tools & Joints
modules.description: The families of wood joint, how a joint is marked out and cut, and how members are fastened and assembled.

units.title: Identify joint families and select a joint

criteria.text: Group wood joints into the five families: corner, frame, widening, lengthening and crossing joints.
Name common joints within each family and say what each is used for.
Select a joint for a job, giving a reason from strength, appearance and the direction of load.
Explain why a widening joint is used for a table top and a lengthening joint for a truss member.
Work from the face side and face edge for every measurement, and never from a damaged or unprepared end.
Square a shoulder line across the face and down both edges with a try square, continuing the line without stepping.
criteria.evidence: Assessor sign-off; lines checked for step.

criteria.text: Set a marking gauge to a stated dimension and gauge the cheek lines from the face side on both members.
criteria.evidence: Gauge setting checked; marked stock inspected.

criteria.text: Mark the waste clearly on the correct side of every line before any cut is made.
Saw on the waste side of the line, leaving the line on the work.
criteria.evidence: Cut inspected against the line; assessor sign-off.

criteria.text: Start a tenon saw cut with the saw held at a low angle and the thumb guiding the blade clear of the teeth.
Saw down to the shoulder line square in both planes, checking the far face as the cut proceeds.
criteria.evidence: Cut checked with try square; assessor sign-off.

criteria.text: Pare waste to the line with a chisel, cutting from both faces towards the middle so the edge does not break out.

units.title: Fasten members with nails, screws and glue

criteria.text: Select a nail for a job from its head and section: wire nail for rough work, oval brad where splitting must be avoided, lost head where the head is to be punched and filled, panel pin for light work with glue.
Apply the rule that two thirds of a fastener's length should enter the lower member, and pre-drill in hardwood or near an end to avoid splitting.
criteria.evidence: Work inspected for splitting; written test.

criteria.text: Select a screw by head type for the job: countersunk flush in woodwork, round head for fittings without countersunk holes, coach screw tightened with a spanner for heavy work.
Apply glue evenly and sparingly so that it does not spill over when the joint is cramped up.
Dry-fit a joint before glue is applied and correct the fit rather than forcing it.
Explain why an over-tight tenon splits the mortise and a slack one gives a weak joint.
Cramp up an assembly square, checking by measuring both diagonals.
Clean up the assembled work and inspect it against the drawing before it is passed on.
